newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian official wants changes to major arms pact.
newsitem.headline: Russian official wants changes to major arms pact.

text.p: A senior Defence Ministry official, quoted by Interfax news agency, said on Tuesday that major changes were needed to the keynote START-2 strategic arms reduction treaty before Russia could ratify it.
The agency quoted the official as saying that "quantitative and qualitative" changes should be made to the nuclear arms pact, which was signed by the U.S. and Russian presidents in 1993.
He expected the Russian ministry to raise the issue when U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry visits Moscow this week.

But a spokesman for Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said he had no information about any Russian demands to amend the treaty, which would slash Russian and U.S. nuclear arsenals to one third of their Cold War levels.
"This is a personal opinion of Interfax's source. We at the defence ministry do not have any information of this kind," Viktor Boronets said by telephone.

START-2, signed by President Boris Yeltsin and then U.S. leader George Bush at a Kremlin ceremony in January 1993, would require the United States and Russia to cut their nuclear stocks to between 3,000 and 3,500 long-range warheads each by the year 2003.
Perry, due in Moscow on Wednesday, will press Russia's State Duma (lower house) to ratify the pact.
The U.S. Senate ratified it last January, but the document is likely to face a rougher ride in the Duma which is dominated by communists and their allies.
A member of the Duma's foreign affairs committee, quoted by Ekho Moskvy radio, said Perry needed to understand that Russia had financial reasons for delaying ratification.

"He (Perry) understands Russia cannot fulfil the conditions of START-2 within the timeframe laid down because of financial difficulties and we hope that W. Perry will say the Americans are ready to extend the deadline," Vladimir Averchev said.

A senior U.S. defence official said last week that nuclear arsenals were expensive to maintain and added that new cuts, coming at a time of economic and military turmoil in Russia, would free up money for the country's conventional forces.
